strengths: The progression from a universal help action to context-dependent caution and sequential driving provides useful, interpretable testbeds. Researchers studying robust RL and uncertainty estimation have an identifiable reason to be interested.

The experiments demonstrate meaningful behavioral effects: stronger robustness increases help-seeking on novel images, favors actions with smaller potential losses, and reduces driving speed and collisions. The distinction between single-image and all-images optimization is particularly informative.
The performance-difference-lemma argument in Theorem 1 provides a useful foundation for extending state-local regret minimization to discounted continuing MDPs with known transitions.

The appendix supplies substantial experimental detail, sensitivity analyses, and convergence plots. The paper also explicitly acknowledges the limitations of tabular planning and transition certainty.
weaknesses: Necessary—resolve the algorithm–theory mismatch. Algorithms 1 and 2 accumulate positive instantaneous regrets, R <- R + max(0, rho), rather than applying standard regret matching to cumulative signed regrets. These operations are not equivalent, and the printed update need not achieve sublinear regret. For example, a two-action belief assigning probabilities 3/4 and 1/4 to rewards (1,0) and (0,1) produces persistent suboptimal mixing under this update even with k=N=1. Specify which update generated the results, correct the algorithm, and establish that the theoretical guarantees apply to the implementation; affected experiments require re-evaluation if the printed update was used.

Necessary—correct the scope and presentation of the theoretical guarantees. Theorem 3 establishes guarantees for the best or uniformly sampled iterate, whereas the experiments use the last iterate and the surrounding text asserts convergence of the sequence. Appendix C, Eqs. (11)–(13), also contains reversed probability inequalities and a missing negative sign in the exponential. These appear repairable, but the supplied argument needs correction. Additionally, the state-space-independent computational-cost statement on page 5 conflicts with the tabular policy evaluation described in Section 6 and Appendix B.2.

Necessary—reconcile the empirical narrative with the reported tradeoffs. Table 7 shows that, when help is unavailable, familiar-digit correct-action frequency falls from 99.31% for 10-of-10 to 88.54% for 1-of-20; this substantial cost deserves discussion in the main results. Section 4's claim of less than 2% familiar-image help usage also conflicts with the 2.83% entry in Table 3. Figure 3b supports the emergence of caution with sufficient data, but not a general monotonic increase with training, since help-seeking decreases between 10% and 100% training data.

Necessary—revise categorical claims about related approaches. Deterministic rewards and fully observed states do not make Bayesian RL inapplicable: uncertainty about an unknown reward function is epistemic even in that setting. Likewise, POMDP formulations can represent uncertainty about latent model parameters. The paper should distinguish its particular deployment protocol and uncertainty objective without dismissing these broader frameworks. Additional competitive benchmarks are not necessary to establish the stated proof-of-concept contribution.

Optional improvements: measure sensitivity to ensemble size and independently retrained ensembles; the reported repetitions primarily vary ordering within one trained ensemble. For driving, reporting progress and collisions per distance alongside the current statistics would clarify the tradeoff between avoiding collisions and approaching a stopped policy. These additions would strengthen practical interpretation, but the unresolved algorithmic and reporting issues above are the basis for leaning reject.
